newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turk minister calls for southeast security reform.
newsitem.headline: Turk minister calls for southeast security reform.

text.p: Turkish deputy prime minister Bulent Ecevit called on Tuesday for substantial changes to security arrangements in the mainly Kurdish southeast where guerrillas are fighting for independence or autonomy.

Ecevit said emergency rule enforced in nine southeastern provinces could be lifted within months if certain conditions were met and called for changes in the "village guard" militia system, Anatolian news agency said.

"On the condition there is the necessary cooperation between the security forces ... and the government departments, it will be possible to end emergency rule within the year," the state-run agency quoted Ecevit as saying.
"The reform of the village guard system and the beginning of the process of change to another system was agreed in principle," he said.

Ecevit was speaking after a meeting of the government's High Commission on the Fight against Terrorism. The commission's decisions are not binding and must be approved by both the cabinet and the military-dominated National Security Council.

Emergency rule, one step short of martial law, has been in force in the nine southeastern provinces since 1987. The rule gives police and security forces wide powers of arrest and detention in their fight against Kurdish rebels in the area.

Turkey has more than 60,000 village guards employed in the fight with Kurdish rebels of the Kurdistan Workers Party (PKK). The media has accused village guards of extortion and involvement in private blood feuds and the drugs trade.
Two men were killed on Tuesday when rebel Kurds attacked a village in eastern Turkey, Anatolian said.
It said PKK guerrillas attacked Bozcali village in Erzincan province, killing the village headman and a 70-year-old man.
In a separate incident, seven Turkish soldiers were injured on Tuesday when their jeep struck a land-mine near the village of Narlikoy in Diyarbakir province, security officials said.
More than 26,000 people have been killed in the 13-year conflict between the Turkish armed forces and the PKK.
